title: Neo-Hittite states
capsule: The Neo-Hittite states were a group of Luwian-speaking and Aramean successor principalities in southeastern Anatolia and northern Syria that preserved elements of Hittite imperial culture after the collapse of the Hittite New Kingdom around 1180 BCE. Major centers included Carchemish, Malatya (Melid), Sam'al, Gurgum, and Patina (Unqi), each ruled by local dynasties who commissioned monumental sculptures and hieroglyphic Luwian inscriptions well into the Iron Age. The Assyrian empire systematically conquered these polities: Carchemish fell to Sargon II in 717 BCE, and by around 700 BCE all the principal Neo-Hittite states had been absorbed as Assyrian provinces.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The locations of most Neo-Hittite capitals are archaeologically identified; territorial boundaries between individual states are partially attested by border stelae and Assyrian campaign records but remain approximate, especially for the earliest phase (1150–1000 BCE).
